newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Samsung opens $847 million Malaysian complex.
newsitem.headline: Samsung opens $847 million Malaysian complex.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Group opened a 2.1 billion ringgit ($847 million) complex in Malaysia on Monday and proposed more investments as the electronics industry recovers from a global slump.

Yun Jong Yong, president and chief executive officer of Samsung Electronics Co Ltd, said Samsung Group planned to invest another 727.5 million ringgit by the year 2000 in the complex of three factories.

The site, in the southwestern state of Negeri Sembilan, is the Samsung Group's largest overseas electronics manufacturing complex and will produce computer monitors and tubes for television and computer monitors.
It consists of three integrated manufacturing facilities for Samsung Electron Devices (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd, Samsung Corning (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd and Samsung Electronic Display Sdn Bhd.

The conglomerate aimed to increase annual turnover from the complex to two trillion won ($2.33 billion) in the year 2000 from this year's target of $1.3 billion, the Samsung Group said in a statement released in Seoul.
Samsung (Malaysia) managing director Kim Jin-ki told Reuters the company was encouraged by signs the electronics industry was beginning to recover from last year's global slump.
"We certainly see a growth in the industry and although demand is still flat, we're encouraged by this," Kim said.
Samsung also hoped to penetrate the Indian market in an attempt to widen its Asian operations, now in 11 countries.
"All we know about India now is that it's a big potential market and we have to study what we can do there," he said.
About $900 million, or 45 percent, of Samsung's investments in Asia are now in Malaysia, Kim said,
"Actually Malaysia has the best resources, social and political stability and infrastructure to suit our needs at the moment," he said.
"But we're slightly concerned about the shortage of its labour, especially high-tech engineers."
Electronics and electrical equipment account for some 15 percent of Malaysia's export earnings.
The government is worried labour shortages and escalating wages in the industry are making Malaysia less competitive than countries such as Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and China.
As a result, Malaysia is seeking to rely less on low-cost assembly of electronic components and chips and attract investment in research, software and design, and other higher value-added products.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said at the complex's opening that Samsung was a model for the kind of high-technology, valued-added investment Malaysia was seeking.

He said Malaysia's industrial policy stressed semiconductor manufacturing and high-end computer components, digital equipment, professional and industrial equipment and multimedia software. ($1 = 2.48 ringgit)
